summary: No Córdoba-specific legal, enforcement, or incident finding is documented. A trans visitor to Córdoba stands under Colombia's national framework and is assessed against the national position rather than against any local deviation.
tangentialFactors:
Documented anti-trans violence in Colombia is concentrated in other departments. In Bello, Antioquia, Sara Millerey was attacked in daylight on 4 April 2025; the assault was filmed, the video circulated from 5 April, and she died of cardiac arrest that afternoon. Police questioned local residents, and no arrest had been made even after the president ordered an urgent investigation. The case illustrates a pattern in which a lethal attack takes place in daylight, is recorded, and leaves the perpetrator unarrested. The same reporting notes earlier killings of gay men and the stabbing death of a trans rough-sleeper.

National counts recorded in that reporting: 13 trans people killed by hate in the first quarter of 2025; eight trans women killed between February and April 2024; 41 trans women killed in 2023. These are raw totals for the whole country, not for Córdoba, and the source inventory carries no general homicide rate for comparison, so no per-capita or relative-risk figure can be derived from them.

In Caquetá, armed groups have run a "social cleansing" campaign: flyers distributed on the streets and by WhatsApp named "faggots, lesbians and men and women who destroy homes" as legitimate military targets. A trans woman who was a local election candidate was told by three armed men that she had one week to leave town; she hid for a week and fled at night. A second trans woman said a friend had been killed. Discrimination in that department leaves trans women few options beyond hairdressing or sex work.
localsOnly:
For trans people living in Córdoba, no department-level protection, enforcement, or incident finding is documented; the national framework and national protection machinery apply. The documented pattern of armed-actor threat campaigns and displacement in other departments is a resident-facing risk, since a person living in an affected area faces displacement rather than departure at will; the Caquetá cases record trans women given a deadline to leave and fleeing at night.

In Caquetá, discrimination confines trans women largely to hairdressing or sex work, a labour-market condition that bears on residents rather than on short-stay visitors. No equivalent Córdoba-specific finding is documented.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Córdoba-specific data on enforcement, incidents, protection orders, or access to facilities was identified in the source inventory. Whether armed-group threat campaigns of the kind documented in Caquetá operate in Córdoba is not sourced.

The national killing counts cited here are raw totals. The inventory contains no general homicide rate for Colombia, so no comparison between trans-specific killings and background violence can be made, and the counts cannot be presented as a rate.

No department-level breakdown of the national counts is available, so the share attributable to Córdoba is unknown.
